Introduction¶

In this lab, you will select a prediction task to perform on your dataset, evaluate two different deep learning architectures and tune hyper-parameters for each architecture. If any part of the assignment is not clear, ask the instructor to clarify.

Dataset Selection¶

Select a dataset similarly to lab one. That is, the dataset must be table data and must have categorical features. In terms of generalization performance, it is helpful to have a large dataset for building a wide and deep network. It is also helpful to have many different categorical features to create the embeddings and cross-product embeddings. It is fine to perform binary classification, multi-class classification, or regression. You are NOT allowed to use the census (i.e., Adult) dataset that was given as an example in class.

Stratified shuffle split is an ideal choice for datasets with imbalanced classes because it maintains the proportion of each class in both training and test sets, ensuring that the model learns to generalize across all classes. It also introduces randomness to reduce potential bias from the order in which data is presented, leading to a more robust evaluation of the model's performance on unseen data.

Modeling (5 points total)¶

Create Wide and Deep Networks (2 points)¶

  • Create at least three combined wide and deep networks using Keras.
  • Visualize the performance of each network on the training data and validation data in the same plot versus the training iterations.
In [ ]:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Input, Dense, Embedding, Dropout, BatchNormalization, concatenate
from tensorflow.keras.models import Model

def create_wide_and_deep_model(num_features, num_deep_layers=3, deep_units=64):
    # Wide input part
    wide_input = Input(shape=(num_features,), name='wide_input')
    
    # Deep input part
    deep_input = Input(shape=(num_features,), name='deep_input')
    x = deep_input
    for i in range(num_deep_layers):
        x = Dense(deep_units, activation='relu', name=f'deep_layer_{i+1}')(x)
        # x = Dropout(0.5, name=f'dropout_{i+1}')(x)  # Adding dropout to prevent overfitting
        x = BatchNormalization(name=f'batch_norm_{i+1}')(x)  # Adding batch normalization to improve training stability

    # Combine wide and deep parts
    combined = concatenate([wide_input, x], name='concatenate_layer')
    outputs = Dense(1, activation='sigmoid', name='output_layer')(combined)  # Output layer
    
    # Create the model object
    model = Model(inputs=[wide_input, deep_input], outputs=outputs)
    
    # Compile the model
    model.compile(optimizer='adam', 
                  loss='binary_crossentropy', 
                  metrics=['Recall']) 

    return model

So with this lab and data, I want to make the most "basic" model possible and see where I can take it. I am going to start with no wide components and just a few processes in my deep layers.

In [ ]:
# Function to build, train, and evaluate the model
def build_model(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, num_deep_layers=3, deep_units=64):
    num_features = X.shape[1]
    model = create_wide_and_deep_model(num_features, num_deep_layers, deep_units)
    history = model.fit([X_train, X_train], y_train, validation_data=([X_test, X_test], y_test), epochs=10, batch_size=32, verbose=0)
    return model, history
In [ ]:
# Function to evaluate the model using Repeated K-Fold cross-validation
def evaluate_model(X, y, build_model_func):
    num_features = X.shape[1]
    recall_scores = []
    fold_number = 0

    # Create the StratifiedShuffleSplit object
    sss = StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=4, test_size=0.4, random_state=42)

    # Get indices for training and test sets
    # splitting using indices from StratifiedShuffleSplit
    for train_index, test_index in sss.split(X, y):
        X_train, X_test = X.iloc[train_index], X.iloc[test_index]
        y_train, y_test = y.iloc[train_index], y.iloc[test_index]

        model, history = build_model_func(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test)

        # Visualization for each fold
        plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
        plt.subplot(2, 2, 1)
        plt.plot(history.history['Recall'], label='Train Recall')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.ylabel('Recall')
        plt.title('Recall Over Epochs - Training')
        plt.legend()

        plt.subplot(2, 2, 2)
        plt.plot(history.history['val_Recall'], label='Validation Recall')
        plt.title('Recall Over Epochs - Validation')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.legend()

        plt.subplot(2, 2, 3)
        plt.plot(history.history['loss'], label='Training Loss')
        plt.ylabel('Loss')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.title('Loss Over Epochs - Training')
        plt.legend()

        plt.subplot(2, 2, 4)
        plt.plot(history.history['val_loss'], label='Validation Loss')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.title('Loss Over Epochs - Validation')
        plt.legend()

        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

        # Compute recall at the end of the fold
        test_recall = recall_score(y_test, (model.predict([X_test, X_test]) > 0.5).astype(int), average='weighted')
        recall_scores.append(test_recall)
        print(f'Fold {fold_number} Test Recall: {test_recall:.3f}')
        fold_number += 1

    average_recall = np.mean(recall_scores)
    print(f"Average Recall across all folds: {average_recall:.3f}")
    return recall_scores

Overfitting Indication: The model is likely overfitting since the training recall is nearly perfect, but the validation recall is much lower. This suggests it's memorizing the training data without learning to generalize.

Loss Graph Anomalies: The training and validation loss both decrease, but it’s unusual that validation loss is consistently lower than training loss, which may indicate an issue with loss calculation or data handling.

Flat Validation Recall: The validation recall is unusually consistent, hinting at potential issues with the validation process or recall calculation.

Low Test Recall: The very low test recall underscores the model's poor generalization to new data.

Model Structure: The model combines wide and deep elements, which theoretically balances memorization with generalization. However, the deep layers may be overly regularized with dropout and batch normalization, possibly causing underperformance.

Potential Improvements:

Crossing Columns: Adding wide network features like crossing columns could help the model learn feature interactions better.
L1/L2 Regularization: Implementing these in the deep layers might combat overfitting by penalizing complexity.

Investigate Generalization Performance (2 points)¶

  • Alter the number of layers in the deep branch of the network and evaluate the performance.
  • Compare the models using the chosen cross-validation method and evaluation metric to determine the superior model.
  • Use proper statistical methods to compare different models’ performance.
In [ ]:
import numpy as np
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Input, Dense, Embedding, Dropout, BatchNormalization, concatenate, Lambda
from tensorflow.keras.models import Model
import tensorflow as tf

def create_wide_and_deep_model_2(cross_col_X_names, categorical_headers_ints, numeric_headers, X_train, X_test):
    # Crossed columns
    input_crossed = Input(shape=(X_train[cross_col_X_names].shape[1],), dtype='int64', name='crossed_input')
    crossed_outputs = []
    for idx, col in enumerate(cross_col_X_names):
        combined_series = pd.concat([X_train[col], X_test[col]])
        N = len(np.unique(combined_series))
        N_reduced = int(np.sqrt(N))
        x = Embedding(input_dim=N, output_dim=N_reduced, input_length=1, name=f'{col}_embed')(input_crossed[:, idx])
        crossed_outputs.append(x)
    wide_branch = concatenate(crossed_outputs, name='wide_concat')

    # Categorical columns
    input_cat = Input(shape=(X_train[categorical_headers_ints].shape[1],), dtype='int64', name='cat_input')
    cat_outputs = []
    for idx, col in enumerate(categorical_headers_ints):
        combined_series = pd.concat([X_train[col], X_test[col]])
        N = len(np.unique(combined_series))
        N_reduced = int(np.sqrt(N))
        x = Embedding(input_dim=N, output_dim=N_reduced, input_length=1, name=f'{col}_embed')(input_cat[:, idx])
        cat_outputs.append(x)
    cat_branch = concatenate(cat_outputs, name='cat_concat')

    # Numeric columns
    input_num = Input(shape=(X_train[numeric_headers].shape[1],), dtype='float32', name='num_input')
    num_branch = Dense(units=20, activation='relu', name='num_dense')(input_num)

    # Combine all deep branch outputs
    deep_branch = concatenate([cat_branch, num_branch], name='deep_concat')
    for i in range(5): 
        deep_branch = Dense(units=64, activation='relu', name=f'deep_layer_{i+1}')(deep_branch)
        deep_branch = Dropout(0.5, name=f'dropout_{i+1}')(deep_branch)
        deep_branch = BatchNormalization(name=f'batch_norm_{i+1}')(deep_branch)

    # Merge the wide and deep branch
    final_branch = concatenate([wide_branch, deep_branch], name='final_concat')
    final_output = Dense(units=1, activation='sigmoid', name='final_output')(final_branch)

    # Create and compile the model
    model = Model(inputs=[input_crossed, input_cat, input_num], outputs=final_output)
    model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['Recall'])

    return model

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

def build_model_2(cross_col_X_names, categorical_headers_ints, numeric_headers, X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, X_train_crossed, X_train_cat, X_train_num, X_test_crossed, X_test_cat, X_test_num):

    # Build the model
    model = create_wide_and_deep_model_2(cross_col_X_names, categorical_headers_ints, numeric_headers, X_train, X_test)
    
    # Train the model
    history = model.fit([X_train_crossed, X_train_cat, X_train_num], y_train, 
                        validation_data=([X_test_crossed, X_test_cat, X_test_num], y_test), 
                        epochs=10, batch_size=32, verbose=0)
    
    return model, history

# Function to evaluate the model using Repeated K-Fold cross-validation
def evaluate_model_2(X, y):
    num_features = X.shape[1]
    recall_scores = []
    fold_number = 0

    # Correct the column names and setup based on actual dataframe usage
    categorical_headers_ints = [
        'Marital_status', 'Nacionality', 'Application_mode', 'Course',
        'Previous_qualification', "Mothers_qualification", "Fathers_qualification",
        "Mothers_occupation", "Fathers_occupation"
    ]

    # Only numeric columns that are not binary, crossed, or categorical
    numeric_headers = [
        col for col in X.columns 
        if X[col].dtype in ['int64', 'float64'] 
        and col not in (categorical_headers_ints + ['Scholarship_holder', 'Debtor', 'Mother_Higher_Ed', 'Father_Higher_Ed', 'Scholarship_Debt_Cross', 'Parent_Qual_Educ_Cross'])
    ]

    cross_col_X_names = ['Scholarship_Debt_Cross', 'Parent_Qual_Educ_Cross']

    # Create the StratifiedShuffleSplit object
    sss = StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=4, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

    # Get indices for training and test sets
    # splitting using indices from StratifiedShuffleSplit
    for train_index, test_index in sss.split(X, y):
        X_train, X_test = X.iloc[train_index], X.iloc[test_index]
        y_train, y_test = y.iloc[train_index], y.iloc[test_index]

        # Prepare the data
        X_train_crossed = X_train[cross_col_X_names].to_numpy()
        X_test_crossed = X_test[cross_col_X_names].to_numpy()
        
        X_train_cat = X_train[categorical_headers_ints].to_numpy()
        X_test_cat = X_test[categorical_headers_ints].to_numpy()
        
        X_train_num = X_train[numeric_headers].to_numpy()
        X_test_num = X_test[numeric_headers].to_numpy()

        model, history = build_model_2(cross_col_X_names, categorical_headers_ints, numeric_headers, X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, X_train_crossed, X_train_cat, X_train_num, X_test_crossed, X_test_cat, X_test_num,)

        # Visualization for each fold
        plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
        plt.subplot(2, 2, 1)
        plt.plot(history.history['Recall'], label='Train Recall')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.ylabel('Recall')
        plt.title('Recall Over Epochs - Training')
        plt.legend()

        plt.subplot(2, 2, 2)
        plt.plot(history.history['val_Recall'], label='Validation Recall')
        plt.title('Recall Over Epochs - Validation')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.legend()

        plt.subplot(2, 2, 3)
        plt.plot(history.history['loss'], label='Training Loss')
        plt.ylabel('Loss')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.title('Loss Over Epochs - Training')
        plt.legend()

        plt.subplot(2, 2, 4)
        plt.plot(history.history['val_loss'], label='Validation Loss')
        plt.xlabel('Epoch')
        plt.title('Loss Over Epochs - Validation')
        plt.legend()

        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

From these charts, it's apparent that the model isn't generalizing well to new data; the fluctuating validation recall suggests as much. It seems to excel with the training data but fails to maintain this performance on the validation set. This disparity might hint at overfitting, with the model latching onto specifics in the training set that aren’t broadly applicable. I'm considering adjusting the complexity of the model or its learning rate, and possibly revisiting the feature set, to address this inconsistency. It's clear some further refinement is necessary to improve the model's predictive reliability.
